systems.name: One equation for change, drawn as strokes
systems.summary: An equation that gives, for every value and every moment, how fast a quantity changes. Drawn as short strokes, it shows the shape of every possible answer before anything is calculated

blocks.label: The equation
blocks.note: The unknown is a curve x(t): the value of a quantity x at each moment t. The rule f gives how fast x changes, written dx/dt, for each value of x and each moment. The second part, x(t0) = x0, fixes the start: at the moment t0 the value is x0

blocks.label: Separable equations, solved by integrating both sides
blocks.note: Sometimes the rate is a part that depends only on x, written g(x), times a part that depends only on t, written h(t). Then the two parts can be moved to opposite sides. The sign ∫ means integrating: adding up very many small pieces into a total. Integrating each side gives the answer. The constant C is fixed by the starting value

blocks.label: Linear equations of first order, solved with an integrating factor
blocks.tex: x' + a(t)x = b(t), \qquad x(t) = e^{-A(t)}\!\left(\int\! e^{A(t)}b(t)\,dt + C\right),\; A = \!\int\! a
blocks.note: x' is the rate of change of x. First order means that only this rate appears, not the rate of the rate. a(t) and b(t) depend only on time, and A is the integral of a. The answer has two parts: the start, fading with time, plus the response to the outside push b(t)

blocks.label: Linear with constant coefficients, solved by its characteristic equation
blocks.note: x'' is the rate of change of the rate, the acceleration. The equation describes a spring with friction: ω (omega) sets how fast it swings, ζ (zeta) how strong the friction is. Trying x = e^(λt) turns it into the quadratic equation for λ on the right. Real roots give a growth or a decay. Complex roots, which contain the square root of -1, give an oscillation

blocks.label: Where the formulas stop
blocks.note: The equation of a pendulum: θ (theta) is the angle from the vertical, g the pull of gravity, L the length of the string. For small angles sin θ is close to θ and a formula exists. For large angles no formula built from the usual functions solves it. This is why such equations are solved numerically, in small steps

dimension.label: What a solution is
dimension.note: A solution is a curve x(t) whose rate of change equals the rule f at every moment. The sign ≡ means equal for every t. The only sure check is to put the curve into the equation and see that both sides agree

systems.name: Solving an equation step by step
systems.summary: When no formula gives the answer, it is built in small steps: read the rate of change, move a little, repeat. The size of the step decides how close the result stays to the true answer

blocks.label: Euler's method: follow the rate for one step
blocks.note: x_n is the value after n steps, t_n the time then, and h the length of a step. The rule f gives the rate at the current point. Euler's method moves along that rate in a straight line for one step. In words: new value = old value + step × rate

blocks.label: The midpoint method: read the rate again halfway
blocks.note: First a trial half step is taken with Euler's method. The rate is read again at that halfway point, and the full step uses this second rate

blocks.label: The fourth-order Runge-Kutta method, the one most used
blocks.tex: x_{n+1} = x_n + \frac{h}{6}\left(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4\right),\qquad\begin{aligned} k_1 &= f(x_n, t_n) \\ k_2 &= f(x_n + \tfrac{h}{2}k_1,\; t_n + \tfrac{h}{2}) \\ k_3 &= f(x_n + \tfrac{h}{2}k_2,\; t_n + \tfrac{h}{2}) \\ k_4 &= f(x_n + h k_3,\; t_n + h) \end{aligned}
blocks.note: The rate is read four times inside each step: k1 at the start, k2 and k3 at the middle, k4 at the end. The step uses their average, with the two middle readings counted twice

blocks.label: The order of a method
blocks.note: e(h) is the error at the end of a run with step h. A method has order p when the error is proportional to h to the power p, written O(h^p). Then halving the step divides the error by 2 to the power p. Measured on a swing whose exact motion is known: 1.03 for Euler, 2.00 for midpoint, 4.00 for Runge-Kutta

blocks.label: What a method can fail to keep
blocks.note: For a swing without friction, x is the position and v the speed. Its energy E stays the same for ever. Over a hundred turns at a step of 0.01, Euler's method ends with an energy of 267.67 where the true value is 0.5. Runge-Kutta ends with 0.500000

dimension.label: The order, measured rather than assumed
dimension.note: log2 is the logarithm to base 2: the power to which 2 must be raised. The run must end exactly after a whole number of swings. Otherwise the small mismatch in the end time adds an error larger than the method's own

systems.name: Two quantities at once: the phase plane
systems.summary: Two quantities that change together, such as the position and the speed of a swing. Their pair of values is drawn as one point, and its history as one curve

blocks.label: The system
blocks.note: The bold x is a list of numbers that together make the state. Here there are two of them, so the state is a point in the plane, written ℝ². The dot over x means its rate of change. One rule f gives the rate of every number in the list

blocks.label: An equation with an acceleration, rewritten as two equations
blocks.tex: x'' = g(x, x') \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \begin{cases} \dot{x} = v \\ \dot{v} = g(x, v)\end{cases}
blocks.note: x'' is the acceleration, the rate of change of the speed. Calling the speed a second unknown, v, turns one equation into two, each with only a first rate. Nothing else changes

blocks.label: A rest point, and the straight-line picture near it
blocks.note: x* is a point where the rule gives zero rate, so a state placed there stays. J, the Jacobian, is a table: how fast each rate f_i changes when each number x_j moves a little. Near the rest point the motion is close to that of a simpler linear system built from J, as a curve near a point is close to its tangent line

blocks.label: The two numbers that classify a rest point
blocks.note: λ1 and λ2 are the eigenvalues of J: the two growth rates of the straight-line picture. τ is the sum of the diagonal entries of J and Δ its determinant. Both real and of the same sign: a node, where states go straight in or out. Real and of opposite signs: a saddle, in along one line and out along another. Complex, containing the square root of -1: a spiral. Purely imaginary: a centre, where the straight-line picture cannot decide what the real system does

blocks.label: Area, and whether it shrinks
blocks.note: ∇·f, the divergence, adds up how fast each rate grows with its own number. It equals the rate at which a small patch of states grows or shrinks, as a share of its size V. Only a system whose patches shrink can have an attractor: a set that nearby states settle onto

blocks.label: The van der Pol oscillator, and its limit cycle
blocks.note: μ (mu) sets how strongly the system feeds its own motion. It has one closed loop, called a limit cycle, that nearby paths spiral onto from inside and from outside

blocks.label: Why two quantities are not enough for chaos
blocks.tex: \text{Poincar\'e-Bendixson: a bounded planar orbit tends to an equilibrium or a closed orbit}
blocks.note: This is the Poincaré-Bendixson theorem. In the plane, paths cannot cross. So a path that stays in a bounded region ends at a rest point or on a closed loop. Chaos is therefore impossible with two quantities, and a third one is needed

dimension.label: The classification, from the two eigenvalues
dimension.note: An eigenvalue can have a real part, Re, and an imaginary part, Im, the part multiplied by the square root of -1. The sign of the real part says whether states move in or out. A non-zero imaginary part says that they turn. Both are computed at every rest point that Newton's method finds, not guessed from the picture. Newton's method solves an equation by improving a guess again and again

systems.name: The Lorenz system
systems.summary: Three equations written by Edward Lorenz in 1963 as a much simplified model of a layer of fluid heated from below. Two starts that differ by a tiny amount soon move completely apart. This is chaos, and three quantities are the fewest in which a smooth motion can be chaotic

blocks.label: The three equations
blocks.tex: \begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= \sigma\,(y - x) \\ \dot{y} &= x\,(\rho - z) - y \\ \dot{z} &= x y - \beta z \end{aligned}
blocks.note: x, y and z are the three numbers of the state, and the dot means rate of change. σ (sigma), ρ (rho) and β (beta) are fixed numbers. The usual values are sigma = 10, rho = 28, beta = 8/3

blocks.label: Its rest points
blocks.note: The origin is the fluid at rest. The symmetric pair is a steady roll of the fluid, one in each direction. By rho = 28 all three are unstable, so the state settles at none of them

blocks.label: The volume it loses, everywhere at the same rate
blocks.note: The divergence is the rate at which a small patch of states grows or shrinks. Here it is the same number everywhere, so its value at any point is also its average. Measured at -13.6667

blocks.label: How fast neighbouring states separate
blocks.note: δ(0) is the tiny starting distance between two states, δ(T) the distance after time T, and ln the natural logarithm. λ1, the largest Lyapunov exponent, is the average growth rate of the distance over a long time. Measured at 0.9043 by starting a nearby state and shrinking the distance back each time it grows. The published value is 0.906

blocks.label: How far ahead it can be predicted
blocks.note: δ0 is the starting error, Δ the error at which a prediction becomes useless, and T the time the error takes to get there. A measurement ten times more precise adds ln(10)/0.904, about 2.5 time units, and no more

dimension.label: The Kaplan-Yorke dimension
dimension.note: λ1, λ2 and λ3 are the three Lyapunov exponents: the growth rates of distances in three directions. Their sum equals the divergence. The middle one is zero, because moving along the path neither grows nor shrinks a distance. So the third follows from the other two. D says how much of space the attractor fills: 2 for a surface, 3 for a solid. Measured 2.062, which is the published value. Counting the small boxes needed to cover a finite sample gives 1.911. These are two different definitions of dimension, not a disagreement

systems.name: The Rossler system
systems.summary: Three equations built by Rossler in 1976 to be the simplest system with the same unpredictable behaviour. Two of the equations only add and scale the quantities, and only one term multiplies two of them together

blocks.label: The three equations
blocks.tex: \begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= -y - z \\ \dot{y} &= x + a y \\ \dot{z} &= b + z\,(x - c) \end{aligned}
blocks.note: x, y and z are the three numbers of the state, and the dot means rate of change. a, b and c are fixed numbers, usually a = 0.2, b = 0.2, c = 5.7. The only term that multiplies two of the numbers together is z x

blocks.label: Stretch and fold, as one action
blocks.tex: \text{spiral outward in the } (x,y) \text{ plane} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{lifted by } z \;\longrightarrow\; \text{folded back inward}
blocks.note: The path spirals outward in the flat x-y plane. Far enough out, z lifts it, and it falls back folded towards the middle. Stretching pulls nearby states apart, and folding keeps them in a bounded region. Stretching and folding is what produces chaos, and in this system nothing hides it

blocks.label: The volume it loses, which differs from place to place
blocks.note: The divergence, the rate at which a small patch of states grows or shrinks, is a + x - c. It depends on where the state is, so its value at one point is not the average. At the point (1, 1, 1) it is -4.500, and the average along the attractor is -5.325

blocks.label: A cutting plane that turns the motion into a rule from one crossing to the next
blocks.note: Σ (sigma) is the plane y = 0, counted only when the path crosses it with y growing. P takes each crossing point to the next one. Looking only at the crossings removes one dimension, and it removes the clock too

dimension.label: The Kaplan-Yorke dimension
dimension.note: λ1 is the largest Lyapunov exponent, the growth rate of a small distance, and |λ3| the rate of the strongest shrinking. A measured λ1 of 0.0702 (published 0.0714) and a measured average divergence of -5.325 give D = 2.013, against a published 2.01

systems.name: The logistic map
systems.summary: A rule that turns one number into the next, applied over and over. One number is enough for chaos here, where a smooth motion needs three, so everything is quick to compute and to draw

blocks.label: The rule
blocks.note: x_n is the number after n steps, between 0 and 1: for example a population as a share of the largest possible. r is the growth factor. The factor (1 - x_n) slows the growth as the population gets crowded

blocks.label: Its fixed points, and when they hold
blocks.note: A fixed point x* is a number the rule leaves unchanged. f'(x) is the slope of the rule: how much a small change in x is multiplied in one step. A fixed point holds, that is, nearby numbers settle on it, while the size of the slope there is less than 1

blocks.label: A cycle of one rule is a fixed point of another
blocks.note: f^(2) is the rule applied twice. A cycle of two numbers, a to b and back to a, is a fixed point of the rule applied twice. So the test for fixed points also tests cycles, and the doubling of a cycle becomes a calculation

blocks.label: When a cycle doubles, as a condition on the slope
blocks.note: f^(2^n) is the rule applied 2^n times. When its slope at the cycle reaches -1, the cycle stops holding, and a cycle twice as long appears in its place

blocks.label: Superstable: the top of the curve lies on the cycle
blocks.note: At these values R the number 1/2, where the curve of the rule is highest, belongs to the cycle. The cycle is then as stable as it can be. Found by bisection, halving an interval again and again, at R = 2, 3.236068, 3.498562, 3.554641, 3.566667, 3.569244, 3.569795, 3.569913

dimension.label: The Lyapunov exponent of a map
dimension.note: λ is the average, over many steps, of the natural logarithm of the size of the slope at each visited number. It measures how fast nearby numbers move apart. It is negative on a cycle, zero at every doubling, and positive where the sequence is chaotic. At r = 4 it is exactly ln 2, and the measurement gives 0.6931

systems.name: The bifurcation diagram
systems.summary: The rule x → r x (1 - x) turns one number into the next. Its setting r runs along the bottom of one picture, and above each r are all the numbers the sequence keeps returning to. Every change of behaviour shows in that one picture

blocks.label: How it is built
blocks.tex: \text{for each } r: \ \text{iterate, discard the transient, plot what remains}
blocks.note: For each value of r the rule is applied many times. The first steps, before the sequence settles, are thrown away, and the rest are drawn as dots above r. The picture is computed, not drawn by hand

blocks.label: The ways a rest point can change, and why there are few
blocks.note: These short equations, called normal forms, are the simplest examples of each change. Saddle-node: two rest points meet and vanish. Pitchfork: one rest point splits into three. Hopf: the growth rates of a rest point turn from negative to positive in their real part, and a loop grows out of it. Near a single change, every system looks like one of these, which is why the list is so short

blocks.label: The doublings, and the constant in their gaps
blocks.note: R_n is the value of r at the n-th doubling. δ (delta) is the limit of the ratio of each gap between doublings to the next gap. The measured ratios are 4.7089, 4.6808, 4.6630, 4.6684, 4.6690, 4.6692 as the cycle doubles from 4 to 128 values

blocks.label: The same number for another rule, checked rather than assumed
blocks.note: A different rule, whose curve also has a single smooth top. The same code gives 4.6690 for it, and its doublings pile up at r = 0.865571 rather than 3.569913

blocks.label: The second constant, in the widths rather than the gaps
blocks.note: α (alpha) is the factor by which the width of the branches shrinks at each doubling. Where the doublings pile up, the diagram repeats itself on a scale smaller by this factor. A shape that repeats itself at smaller and smaller scales is called a fractal, so here chaos and fractals meet

dimension.label: Feigenbaum's delta, measured on two rules
dimension.note: 4.6692 from the logistic rule and 4.6690 from the sine rule, both computed by the same code

systems.name: A real heart: from the normal beat to a very fast rhythm and back
systems.summary: Half an hour of one recorded human heartbeat, record 207 of the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, a public collection of heart recordings. It is shown as the gaps between beats: the normal rhythm, runs of ventricular flutter (a very fast rhythm of the heart's lower chambers) that start and stop on their own, and a picture of how each gap leads to the next

blocks.label: The gap between beats
blocks.note: t_n is the moment of beat n, and I_n the time from that beat to the next, in milliseconds. The beats are the ones marked by cardiologists on a recording taken 360 times a second. During flutter each flutter wave counts as a beat

blocks.label: The return map
blocks.note: Each gap is drawn against the next one, as a point with I_n across and I_n+1 up. The 1992 experiment on heart tissue used the same picture. A rhythm that repeats gives one spot. A switch between rhythms is a jump from one cloud of points to another

blocks.label: How much one gap says about the next
blocks.note: The gaps are sorted into bins 20 ms wide. σ (sigma) is the spread of a set of values. ρ (rho) divides the average spread of the next gap within one bin by its spread over all beats. ρ = 1 means that knowing a gap does not help guess the next one, and ρ = 0 means the next one follows by a fixed rule. The site's page on the gaps between prime numbers uses the same measure

blocks.label: Beats a minute, from the gaps
blocks.note: Ī is the average gap in milliseconds. A minute has 60,000 milliseconds, so 60000 / Ī is the number of beats a minute. It is worked out separately for the patient's normal rhythm and for the flutter

dimension.label: What the record is
dimension.note: The MIT-BIH collection holds recordings of 47 patients made from 1975 to 1979, free to reuse under the ODC-BY 1.0 licence. Sources: Moody and Mark, IEEE Eng Med Biol 20(3), 2001; Goldberger and colleagues, Circulation 101(23), 2000; PhysioNet doi 10.13026/C2F305. Nothing on the page is generated: every number comes from the recording

definitions.name: An unstable cycle, and control by small nudges
definitions.note: x* = f(x*) says that the rule f brings the state back exactly to x*. |f'(x*)| > 1 says that nearby states move away from it. Such a point is called an unstable periodic orbit. A chaotic attractor, the set a chaotic system keeps moving on, is full of them. That is why a chaotic rhythm keeps passing close to a steady beat that it never keeps. Ott, Grebogi and Yorke showed in 1990 that a small, well-timed change, made whenever the state comes near, can hold it there. Garfinkel, Spano, Ditto and Weiss did this in heart tissue in 1992, with electrical pulses that could only shorten a beat.

definitions.name: The Lyapunov exponent
definitions.note: δ(0) is a tiny starting distance between two states, δ(T) the distance after time T, and ln the natural logarithm. λ is the average rate at which the distance grows. When λ is positive, nearby states separate faster and faster: this is the working definition of chaos. To measure it, the distance is shrunk back each time it grows, so that it never reaches the size of the attractor itself

definitions.name: The divergence of the rule
definitions.note: f_i is the rate of the i-th number of the state, and ∂f_i/∂x_i is how fast that rate changes when the number itself moves a little. Their sum is the rate at which a small patch of states grows or shrinks, as a share of its size V. It also equals the sum of the Lyapunov exponents, so when two exponents are known, the third follows

definitions.name: The Kaplan-Yorke dimension
definitions.note: λ1, λ2 and so on are the Lyapunov exponents, largest first. k is the largest number of them whose sum is not negative. D counts the k whole directions that the stretching keeps open, plus the share of the next direction it reaches. This is the dimension usually quoted for a strange attractor, an attractor with a fractal shape

definitions.name: Box-counting dimension
definitions.note: N(ε) is the number of boxes of side ε needed to cover the set, and d is how fast that number grows as the boxes shrink: 1 for a line, 2 for a surface. The same count measures the roughness of a coastline. On a computed path it works only while the boxes are larger than the gaps between the recorded points. So the fit uses that range of sizes, and the range is reported with the answer

definitions.name: Feigenbaum's constants
definitions.note: δ (delta) is the factor by which each gap between doublings is shorter than the one before. α (alpha) is the factor by which the width of the branches shrinks. The two numbers are the same for every rule whose curve has a single smooth top shaped like a parabola, whatever the rule is otherwise
